newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Major under fire over New Year honours.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Major under fire over New Year honours.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major came under fire on Tuesday over a New Year's honours list the opposition Labour Party said was biased in favour of the ruling Conservatives.
The Daily Telegraph newspaper, normally pro-Conservative, said the prime minister had trivialised the system by focusing too heavily on sports and entertainments personalities.

While business leaders received their due -- London Metal Exchange chairman Raj Bagri becomes a lord and David Rowland, chairman of the Lloyd's insurance market, is knighted -- the main headlines went to the worlds of showbusiness and sport.

Former Beatle Paul McCartney, now Sir Paul, and composer Sir Andrew Lloyd Webber, elevated to the peerage, headed a list of celebrities that included 1960s singer turned game show host Cilla Black and world champion racing driver Damon Hill.

"In proposing what some will see as a surprising number of awards to sports and entertainment personalities, the prime minister risks being accused of further trvialising the honours," the Telegraph said.
The Independent was even more scathing, saying: "It is all a plot to undermine the honours system by ridicule."

The honours system, with titles such as Commander of the Order of the British Empire, dates from the time when Britain did still have an empire. The attraction of a "gong" remains, despite Britain's reduced role in the world.

While entertainers have been honoured in the past, the list has traditionally been a means for the government to reward those who toil in obscure and ill paid positions -- backbench MPs, civil servants and local government worthies.
The Labour Party, however, seized on what it saw as a party political bias in the honours list as the prime minister heads towards a general election, which must be called by May.
It said that in addition to Lloyd Webber, who will now be entitled to vote in the House of Lords, the list was packed with Conservative sympathisers.

"Labour MP Brian Wilson said: "While no-one doubts that Sir Andrew Lloyd Webber is a significant figure in the world of music, the only thing that appears to qualify him to be part of Britain's legislature is that he is an active Tory (Conservative)."
Labour plans radical reform of the unelected upper house of parliament, including an end to the right of hereditary peers to sit and vote there, should it win the general election.
Government officials defended the honours system, saying that 44 percent of the more than 1,000 names of the list were suggested by members of the public.
There was also media criticism of the absence of those caught up in tragedies such as the massacre of 16 children and their teacher at Dunblane, Scotland, last March.
Gallantry honours are not normally included in the New Year's list, but officials said awards were being considered.
